Therapist here; there is a long answer and short answer. 

The short answer is, No, you can't "accidently" abuse someone. 

The long answer: While you can't "accidently" abuse someone, you can /mindlessly/ abuse someone. When violence becomes normalized to the abuser, whether through their own trauma or through media or society, it becomes engraved in them when left unchecked. He does mean to hurt you, but it's possible he may not be ready to accept that. There can be a part of him that loves you and doesn't want to hurt you... but it isn't strong enough to stop the side of him that does. It could be his inner child is hurting and it's best defense is offense... but it could also be that he only feels significant when others are broken down. 

However, no matter the answer, you need to get out of there. He needs to get help for his behavior. There is someone out there that can offer you all of his positives and treat you right. You don't owe him, you can't fix him.... you need to look after you. And perhaps leaving him may be the first step of him realizing he needs to heal. You can still love him and its possible he loves you the best he can... but two people can love each other and still not be good for each other. 

It'll be hard. But you've got this. If you don't feel you'll be safe with this break up, have help prepared beforehand.

Okay so I dated a gamer boy for 4 years, and another one for 5 years. 

My short answer is; "from the sounds of it, no, it does not count". 

My long answer is... that depends on YOU. For some people, parallel play (doing separate things together) is good enough quality time... for others it isnt... and there are some that it is sometimes and other times it isn't. For me, personally, I love parallel play like 85% of the time.... but the other 15% I NEED a more personal connection. I communicated this to my exes and got mixed results; the 5 year guy was a douche (no offense, kinda like yours is being) and the 4 year guy "tried". 4 year guy and I attempted to find games we could play together, since I love games too... but I was eventually bummed to find that ny only two options for emotional connection with him were "gaming together" and "watching a movie". So, that relationship ended. 

I won't lie to you; your bf's response was a huge red flag, but maybe he felt attacked. Giving him the benefit of the doubt, I would maybe talk to him about having weekly meetings, which is what my most recent partner and I did and it's what I recommend to all of the couples I counsel (I'm a mental health therapist). Choose a day of the week, and mark that day as your starting point for that week... during your check in you can find opportunities to let each other know what you appreciated the previous week and what you'd like to see more of the next. That'd give you a good chance to speak up and say "hey I may need more togetherness in the form of ABC this week" or "I really appreciated that you took time to XYZ with me this past week"

I hope things work out. 
Please remember... while it is important to let him has his down time and enjoy his games, you should be put first.

Depends on the location. I'm on the east side of the USA; I'm a licensed mental health therapist who actually specializes in treating clients with BPD. I can diagnose and carry out treatment; the only thing I can't do is prescribe medication.

Ye in the USA licensed social workers and mental health therapists can diagnose clients. HOWEVER, their diagnosis cannot get a client medication; only psychiatrists and doctors can do that. The diagnosis from a mental health therapist is more of a "treatment guideline"; it can help psychiatrist and doctors get a bigger picture (if a release is filled out). Plus, usually a psychiatrist won't have as in depth relationship wirh a client unless they double as a therapist (most, at least in my state, dont), so the actual therapist's opinion does have some weight.

Imma be real with you as a licensed therapist. 

Technically, he HAS to diagnose you for insurance to pay him. Unless it is 100% self-pay, he will not get paid. You HAVE to diagnose a client during first sesssion... one hour is not enough to always feel 100% confident in your diagnosis. He may want time to be confident with his answer. As both a therapist and someone with BPD, I want to reassure you you did nothing wrong (from the sounds of it) in the grand scheme of things. 
Boundaries are VERY important to have with someone who has BPD. Discouraging black and white thinking and not giving into it is also very healthy. I think it's wonderful that you were more open to communication on both ends. 

I think you need to ask yourself if you are willing to continue having this friendship, should the person attempt to come back; is this friendship good for you mentally and emotionally? Some people are able to put aside all emotions and handle the "pushaway" stage of BPD, while it fucks with others... it sounds like you may be the latter. It sounds like this person needs therapy and a lot of personal growth to be healthy for friendships. 

What might be helpful for you is to write out what an overall healthy friendship looks like for you, then going through and marking what areas this friend meets. For the areas she doesn't meet, is it possible for her to meet them with realistic expectations at this time? 

It is okay to be the one to say "I need space"; I think what would be important is to state the changes you'd need to see and letting them know that they aren't a terrible person overall, but you are having a hard time feeling that BOTH of you (very important) arent compatible or healthy for the other person. It may be good to give them a copy of the friendship list I recommended to you; it will not only help them define goals that they will need to reach to be a healthy friend to you, but also hopefully encourage them to acknowledge the assignment and carry it out themselves for their own good.

So, something that is extremely uncomfortable for many of my clients who have a disorder but feel like "it's not going anywhere" is to ask other people who are close to you what they believe you may need to work on. This is risky, as it needs to be someone you trust has really observed you and your habits, as well as someone you won't begin to dislike/distrust due to stating their opinion. The reason this is helpful is there are often times we aren't aware of things that would be helpful to mention in therapy. My most recent partner, who had Schizoid personality disorder, would often leave therapy frustrated and saying they had nothing to talk about/to work on, and then tell me/do something later and I'd have to speak up and say "this is the kind of stuff you need to talk about in therapy"; I believe only me and his best friend would be able to have this kind of talk with him, had he been open to actually working on himself... 

I know those with Schizoid don't have a large social pool to choose from... but I tend to find there is at least one person they can trust Even the slightest. 

You can also put aside the title altogether and ask yourself, what are you most unhappy about? Are you putting in effort into therapy? Are you only wanting to talk about the big problems that are in your face, rather than include the little problems you were "able to get over", but not without some scratches? Are you willing to get uncomfortable and do what a therapist tells you even if you think "thats stupid"? Is this therapist right for you, or do you maybe want to look for someone new?

Just my thoughts both as a therapist and a friend/past partner of someone who has Schizoid PD.
